$comment: Hand-authored plain-language copy per tag (round-2 feedback, thread 858cc161): "tag-name": [summary, description]. Applied by Semtext.Reference.Tags at consolidation and by `mix semtext.export_elements` to the /data/elements.json search index. Edit here, then rebuild + re-export; never hand-edit priv/data/elements.json itself.

agent: Describes one AI agent inside the document: its name, a short bio, and its instructions.
You write name, bio, and instructions as plain children. The browser ignores this element; extraction turns it into one agent record. Use it when the document is addressed to or about an agent.
agent-kit-acceptance-criteria: A given/when/then criteria list for a ticket or story.
You author the criteria; the card renders them as a structured list. Point it at fixtures or an endpoint and it shows the cached snapshot with a last-refreshed stamp.
agent-kit-agent-persona: An agent persona card: who the agent is and how it behaves.
The content you write inside is the record; the card frames it. One renderer serves both persona tags, parameterized by kind.
agent-kit-artifact: A typed artifact card: code or text produced by the work.
You set the type and language and author the content; the card renders it as a cached specimen with a refresh stamp.
agent-kit-asset: A media asset card with a caption.
You point src at the asset, set its mime type and write the caption. The card renders the cached asset; the caption is the record.
agent-kit-board: A kanban-style board laid out over ticket references.
You author the columns and the ticket refs inside; the board renders the layout you wrote. It displays the cached state — it does not poll the tracker.
agent-kit-bug: One renderer serves all six ticket tags, parameterized by type. The inner content you write is the record; the chrome adds the type and the cached state.
agent-kit-chatroom: You author the messages; the card renders the transcript with a cached-snapshot stamp. Refresh is the CLI lane — the embed never fetches at read time.
agent-kit-cucumber: A Gherkin spec card: the feature source shown as written.
You author the spec; the card displays the source verbatim in a cached card. Point it at fixtures for the snapshot stamp.
agent-kit-custom-assert: A list of custom assertions, each an expression and an expectation.
You author the expr and expect pairs; the card renders them as a structured list from the cached snapshot.
agent-kit-cypress: A Cypress spec card: the test source shown as written.
You author the spec; the card displays it verbatim with a last-refreshed stamp from the cached snapshot.
agent-kit-epic: One renderer serves all six ticket tags, parameterized by type. The inner content you write is the record; the chrome adds the type and the cached state.
agent-kit-issue: An issue ticket card with org, project and state.
You set the key, state and labels and write the body; the card renders the cached ticket snapshot. It displays state — it never queries the tracker live.
agent-kit-organization: One renderer serves both reference-card tags, parameterized by kind. The content you write inside is the record.
agent-kit-project: One renderer serves both reference-card tags, parameterized by kind. The content you write inside is the record.
agent-kit-review: A review card: comments and a verdict.
You author the comments and set the verdict; the card renders the cached review. The verdict is data, not a live check.
agent-kit-sub-task: One renderer serves all six ticket tags, parameterized by type. The inner content you write is the record; the chrome adds the type and the cached state.
agent-kit-task: One renderer serves all six ticket tags, parameterized by type. The inner content you write is the record; the chrome adds the type and the cached state.
agent-kit-test-case: A test-case card: steps and the expectation.
You author the steps and what should happen; the card renders them as a structured list from the cached snapshot.
agent-kit-test-suite: A test-suite card with per-branch rows.
You author the rows — one per branch — and the card renders them from the cached snapshot with a refresh stamp.
agent-kit-ticket-ref: An inline reference to a ticket.
You set the key, org and project; the ref renders as an inline card linking into the ticket family. It stays ordinary text with JavaScript off.
agent-kit-user-persona: A user persona card: who the product serves.
The content you write inside is the record; the card frames it, with an optional avatar. One renderer serves both persona tags.
agent-kit-user-story: One renderer serves all six ticket tags, parameterized by type. The inner content you write is the record; the chrome adds the type and the cached state.
conclusion: The takeaway side of a fact — what the statement means.
You write it inside a sem-fact, after the statement. Flashcard views show it on the answer side; extraction pairs it with the statement.
highlight: Prose with parts the reader can hide to test their recall.
You wrap the words to remember in a highlight child, or use [[double brackets]] as shorthand. Hiding them turns the passage into a self-test; showing them again reveals the answers.
incorrect-statement: A wrong version of a fact, shown so readers can spot the error.
You write it inside a sem-fact. Quiz views can offer it as a wrong answer choice; extraction keeps it labelled as false — never as a claim.
npl-agent: Describes one AI agent: its name, type, and how it should behave.
You write the agent's name, type, and rules as attributes and text. The page shows them as a tidy card. Machines can read the same fields back.
npl-artifact: Shows a piece of work an agent produced, like code or a report, with a title and notes.
Wrap the artifact's title and content in this element and the page adds a frame around them. The content itself is never changed.
npl-cot: Shows the steps of a chain of thought, folded up until the reader opens them.
Each step is listed in order, with the final answer at the end. The list uses a plain details box, so it works even with JavaScript off.
npl-critique: Shows a review of one thing from one point of view: strengths, weaknesses, and a verdict.
You write the subject, the strengths, the weaknesses, and the verdict. The element lays them out as a clean, labelled review card.
npl-declaration: Shows which version of a rules document you are reading.
It renders the version line of an NPL document, such as NPL@1.0, as a banner at the top. Extended documents are marked the same way.
npl-directive: Marks a short instruction inside a sentence, so it stands out from the prose.
You write the instruction, and optionally a longer note, inside this element. The page shows it as a small chip the reader can spot while scanning.
npl-example: A sample element that shows how npl-* elements are built.
It exists to demonstrate the pattern, not to be used in real documents. Real elements replace it.
npl-flag: One setting a reader can switch, shown as a labelled row.
You give it a name and a value. The reader can click the row to apply the setting. If the name implies a number range, values outside it are flagged.
npl-flags: A group of settings shown as clickable rows.
It wraps one or more npl-flag elements. You can add a short note above the rows to explain what they do.
npl-hormones: Shows seven drive levels — like momentum, tension, and curiosity — as bars.
Each drive has a level from 0 to 100, drawn as a bar with an arrow showing whether it rose or fell. Notes explain what a bar means when it passes a set limit.
npl-intent: Shows what a piece of work is meant to achieve: the goal, the scope, and the expected outcomes.
You write the goal, what is in and out of scope, the outcomes, and any assumptions. The element lays them out in a clear grid so a reader can check the plan at a glance.
npl-mindread: Shows what one party thinks another party believes or feels.
You write the subject, the signals (tone, patterns, things left unsaid), and the reading drawn from them. The result is clearly labelled as a guess, not a fact.
npl-mode: Lists the thinking styles an agent uses, one chip per style.
You write each mode as a child element. The main mode is marked so the reader knows which lens leads. This element only shows information; it changes nothing.
npl-mood: Shows a mood with an emoji, plus an optional note on its tone.
You write the mood in the mood attribute. Extra children can carry the tone, the context, and how the agent will approach work in this mood.
npl-poa: Shows a plan as a decision tree, plus the reasons each path was weighed.
You write the tree, the reasoning with weights, and the option that was picked. The element shows all three parts; it never draws the tree for you.
npl-ref: Looks back at a finished turn: what went well, what to improve, and how it was checked.
You write the assessment, the improvements, the validation, and any eval notes. The element lays them out as a review card after the work.
npl-rubric: A scoring table: each row is a criterion with a weight and a score, plus a total.
You write the criteria, their weights, and their scores. The total is shown as given, or worked out from the weights. Wrong or missing numbers are flagged, not hidden.
npl-section: A labelled section for any NPL prompt block.
Known section types get a matching header; unknown types get a warning style so a typo is easy to spot. The content stays plain text, so search and copy still work.
npl-thought: A thought bubble: short related ideas grouped under one type.
Each child is one thought with a type attribute, such as a question or a risk. The element shows them as a tidy list of bubbles.
npl-vos: Shows a persona's inner state: id, ego, superego, and mood, before a reply.
You write each part of the state. The element shows them as labelled parts of one bracket. An optional collective part covers group personas.
sem-api-call: Documents one API call's contract: method, endpoint, status and its parameters, as a card.

The definition card for an endpoint. You write the operation name, HTTP method and path, then one sem-api-param child per parameter or response field; the page shows a table and machines read the same fields back.
sem-api-param: One parameter row inside a sem-api-call: name, where it lives, type and description.
The child of sem-api-call. The in attribute says where the parameter lives (query, body, header, or response for a returned field); required marks the ones the caller must send.
sem-audiences: Names the reader groups a document knows about, so each reader sees the parts meant for them.
You list each group here, then mark sections with an audience attribute. The reader picks their group and the page hides the rest. Nothing is deleted — machines still read the whole document.
sem-browser: Draws a browser-style window around a live SemText document.
It gives the document an address bar and a window frame, while everything inside stays real, working SemText. Use it when a page demonstrates a document rather than being one.
sem-changelog: A changelog: dated entries describing what changed.
You wrap the collection in sem-changelogs and write one entry per change inside, each with its date and a name. It stays ordinary readable text with JavaScript off.
sem-changelogs: The collection wrapper for changelog entries.
You set the kind — added, changed, fixed, removed — on each entry, and the chrome labels the collection. The entries themselves are the record; nothing is invented.
sem-chronology: A timeline: dated events shown in the order they happened.

Each child is one event with a when date, an optional end date, and an optional status. You write the events in order; the element never sorts them. It can show the events as a timeline rail or as a plain list.
sem-code: A code listing with a file name, a language, and marked lines.
The code is shown exactly as written — spacing included. You can mark the lines that matter, and the reader gets copy controls a plain code block cannot offer.
sem-data-join: Combines two named data sets on one shared column, like a database join.
You name the two sources and the key column. The joined result becomes a new data set that queries can use. Nothing shows on the page by itself — it only feeds queries.
sem-data-query: A question asked of a data set, written in a small, safe SQL-like language.
You write one query: pick columns, filter, sort, and limit. Joins are declared separately, and nothing can change the data. Readers see the results, and the query text stays visible.
sem-data-source: One named set of data inside a data visualizer.
You either write the data inside the element or point at a file with source. Doing both is an error the element reports clearly. With JavaScript off, the data still reads as text.
sem-data-visualizer: The container that holds data sets, joins, and queries, and shows the results.

You put one or more sem-data-source children inside, plus any joins and queries. The container owns the shared state: which data set and query are active. With JavaScript off it shows the data as plain tables.
sem-detail: One passage of prose with parts that can be hidden for self-testing.
This is the child of sem-details. Wrap the words to recall in a highlight, or use [[double brackets]]. Hiding them turns the passage into a memory exercise.
sem-details: A group of passages whose key words can be hidden for recall practice.
Each sem-detail child is one passage. Readers hide or show the highlighted words to test themselves. This is a study aid — not a reveal box and not a tab set.
sem-enhanced-document: The required root wrapper around a SemText document.
You wrap the whole document in it once. Inside, plain HTML and sem-* elements mix freely. Extraction reads everything inside the wrapper; the browser treats it as an ordinary container.
sem-eval: An evaluation spec: the inputs, expected outputs and criteria in one container.
You author the cases as sections or prose inside; the container adds the chrome and label. It states what a good answer looks like — it does not run anything.
sem-event: One dated event on a timeline.
You give it a when date, an optional until end date, and an optional status such as planned or done. Its place in the page is its place in time — the element does not sort events.
sem-fact: One fact: a statement, its conclusion, and optionally what would be wrong to believe.
You write the statement, the conclusion drawn from it, and any incorrect-statement to warn against. The id is the token other text cites. It reads as plain sentences with JavaScript off.
sem-facts: A group of facts the reader can flip through as cards, a quiz, or plain prose.
You wrap sem-fact children in it and pick a view with view-as. The view only changes how the facts are shown — the facts themselves stay the same, and machines always read all of them.
sem-faq: One FAQ entry: the asked question and its authored answer.
The question child is the question; everything you write in the answer child is the answer. Machines extract both verbatim; the browser can show them as a Q and A pair.
sem-faqs: You wrap sem-faq children in it. The view only changes how the questions and answers are shown — the words stay the same.
sem-file-tree: A file listing written as an indented tree inside a pre block.

You type the tree with box-drawing characters or plain indentation; with JavaScript on the same engine as sem-site-tree turns it into a browsable listing, and with JavaScript off the pre is the record.
sem-guard-rail: One guard rail: a rule the reader should not cross.
You give it a severity and a scope, and write the rule as the content. It renders as a labelled, warning-level item in the guard-rails list.
sem-guard-rails: You wrap sem-guard-rail children in it. The collection sorts nothing and invents nothing — the rails you wrote, in the order you wrote them.
sem-howto: A how-to guide container: a named guide with free contents.
The name child is the title; everything else inside is the guide. The container adds the chrome and label — you write the steps with the elements you already have.
sem-kb: A knowledge-base article: the content you write inside is the article.
There is no special structure to learn — headings, prose and the other elements all work as usual. The container frames the article with a labelled panel.
sem-md: A block written in Markdown that the browser turns into HTML.

You write tables, lists, and other Markdown inside the element. Readers see a formatted table or list; machines get the Markdown back unchanged. Made for content that is easier to write as Markdown than as HTML.
sem-mockup: A UI mockup container holding text or HTML.
You pick the mode — text or html — and put the mockup inside. It renders as a framed specimen; nothing inside it is interactive.
sem-note: A callout: a short piece of prose set beside the main text.
Pick a variant — info, warning, tip, or danger — for the colour and label. The collapsed attribute hides the body behind a short teaser. It stays ordinary readable text with JavaScript off.
sem-option: One answer choice in a question.
The correct attribute marks the right choice. Readers pick an answer; machines read which option was correct.
sem-philosophy: A principles container: the beliefs or rules a project runs on.
You write the principles inside as prose or lists. The container gives them a labelled home so machines can find the project's stated principles.
sem-plan: A plan container: the reasoning and the steps of a solution.
You write the plan inside as sections or prose, with an optional status. The container keeps the reasoning with the work it produced.
sem-procedure: An ordered list of steps, each marked with where it stands.
You write one sem-step per step, in the order they happen. Each step carries a status: done, current, todo, or blocked. There are no step numbers to maintain — position is the number.
sem-profile: Names one reader group inside a sem-audiences block.
You give it an id and a short label. Sections tagged with this id show or hide as the reader switches groups.
sem-progress: A progress bar for one number between 0 and 1.
You give it a value and an optional label. The page draws a bar with the percentage. Values outside the range are clamped for display, and the raw value still reads as text without JavaScript.
sem-properties: A list of key–value pairs, shown as a tidy definition grid.
You write one sem-property per pair. The grid renders with plain CSS, so it works with JavaScript off. Machines read the same pairs back.
sem-property: One key–value pair in a properties grid.
The key attribute is the term; the text inside is its meaning. Add role=definition when the value defines the key.
sem-question: A question with answer choices, for self-testing.
You write the question and one or more sem-option children. It pairs with the quiz views of sem-facts. Works as plain markup with JavaScript off.
sem-reader: Reading tools for a long document: an outline, a progress bar, and controls for text size and theme.
It is page furniture, not content — a document without it loses nothing a machine would read. Readers get focus mode, type size, colour scheme, print, and audience controls in one place.
sem-reference: One numbered entry in a reference list.
You give it an id, a link, and a note. In the text, cite it with a plain link to the id. The element carries the fields a plain list item cannot.
sem-references: A numbered list of sources the document cites.
You wrap one sem-reference per source. Numbers come from position. With JavaScript off the list still reads as an ordinary numbered list.
sem-requirement: A requirement statement with a status and priority.
You write the requirement as the content and set kind, status and priority as attributes. Machines read it as one requirement record; readers see a labelled statement.
sem-reveal: A question the reader clicks to reveal the answer.
You write the question as the summary and the answer as the body. It is a plain details box, so it works with JavaScript off. Use it for explanation — a sem-fact is for claims.
sem-rubric: A scoring rubric container: criteria against levels.
You author the grid inside as a plain table or row prose — the container does not force a shape. Set max-score and the chrome shows the scale.
sem-runbook: An operational runbook: preconditions, procedure and references in one container.
You author the parts inside with the elements you already use; the container adds the chrome and a label. It reads as a document and extracts as one runbook record.
sem-site-tree: A site or file tree written as nested node elements.
You nest bare node children with a path and optional label and kind. The same engine that reads sem-file-tree renders it, so both notations share one model.
sem-source: Lets the reader flip between a section as it renders and the markup behind it.
You put ordinary SemText inside. The reader sees the rendered result, then the exact source that produced it. Made for documents that teach the vocabulary.
sem-step: You write the instruction as the text and set status to done, current, todo, or blocked. Its place in the page is its order in the procedure.
sem-summary: A summary container: the short version of what follows.
Everything you put inside is the record. The container labels it as a summary so skimmers and machines both know what it is.
sem-table: A table the reader can sort and filter — the table you write is the data.
You write a normal HTML table. Sorting and filtering only change what the reader sees; the markup stays the contract, so machines always read the same rows you wrote.
sem-tag-attr: One attribute row inside a sem-tag-def: name, type, required flag, default and description.
The child of sem-tag-def. You write the attribute's name and type, add the required flag when it must be present, and the description text is what readers see in that row.
sem-tag-def: Documents one tag's contract: its attributes, types, defaults and child tags, as a card.

The definition card for a markup tag. You write the tag name and one sem-tag-attr child per attribute; the page shows a tidy table and machines read the same fields back. The reference pages use it, so the vocabulary documents itself.
sem-threat-model: A threat-model container: assets, threats and mitigations.
You author them inside as sections or list prose; the container adds the chrome, label and scope. It frames the analysis — it does not check it.
sem-tldr: A summary block the reader can skim or skip.
Whatever you put inside is the whole record — the element adds nothing and hides nothing. It renders as a set-apart block so the gist is visible at a glance.
sem-tsg: One troubleshooting entry: a symptom and its fix.
You write the problem and the resolution inside; the entry stays ordinary readable text with JavaScript off.
sem-tsgs: You wrap sem-tsg children in it. The collection is the record — the entries you wrote, in the order you wrote them.
sem-view: One named perspective inside a sem-views tab set.
The name attribute labels the tab; the content inside is that view of the subject. With JavaScript off every view shows, each under its name.
sem-views: Shows one subject several ways, with a tab bar to switch.
You wrap sem-view children and name each one. Readers switch by click, keyboard, or link. The content is never moved or rewritten — only which view shows changes.
sem-workflow: An ordered workflow whose steps carry verification.
You write one sem-step per step, like a procedure, plus a duration for the whole run. Each step can carry a gate and check, and an if-no that says what to do when the check fails.
semext-annotate: Visitor comment threads embedded in the page, backed by the annotate service.
The embed renders the cached threads snapshot; it is the one embed of the family with a live anonymous read. Visitors pin comments on the page and the embed shows them in place.
semext-docptr: A doc-pointer card rendered from a cached snapshot.
The snapshot mirrors the pointer registry so a page can cite a source location durably — the card survives line drift until a CLI refresh re-snapshots it.
semext-media-prompt: An authored media-generation prompt with an output cache region.
The record is the prompt you write; the output region beside it is filled by the refresh CLI, not the element. The element never fetches and never generates — it only reports the region's state.
semext-sig-logs: A SigNoz log-line snapshot with a link to open the query.
The log lines you author are the record; the chrome builds an Open in SigNoz anchor from the query, range and env you set. The snapshot is refreshed by the CLI, never fetched at read time.
semext-sig-metrics: A SigNoz metrics snapshot with a link to open the query.
The metrics table you author is the record; the chrome adds the deep link from your query parameters. Nothing is fetched when the page is read.
semext-sig-synthetic-monitor: A SigNoz synthetic-monitor definition card with a deep link.
You author the monitor's expected definition; the card mirrors it and links to SigNoz. Running monitors is a service surface this element deliberately does not touch.
semext-sig-traces: A SigNoz trace-list snapshot with a link to open the query.
The trace list you author is the record; the chrome adds the Open in SigNoz anchor. The embed is cached and link-only — no client queries.
semext-styleguide-theme: One theme's token cards rendered from a cached snapshot.
The card shows the theme name, key color swatches and a type sample, plus a link to preview the theme CSS at the src you set. Refresh is the CLI lane.
semext-styleguide-themes: The collection wrapper for theme token cards.
It renders a summary line over its semext-styleguide-theme children. The snapshots are refreshed by the CLI, not at read time.
statement: The claim side of a fact — what is asserted.
You write the statement as the child of a sem-fact. Its pair, the conclusion, draws the takeaway. Plain text, no attributes needed.
